goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — should_block? uses exact case-sensitive match with no normalization, so a blocked address is bypassed by changing case or adding whitespace (e.g. Spammer@x.com).

app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — Validation performs a DB write (match_count/last_match_at save) as a side effect, so every valid? call mutates state; users_controller#create calls user.valid? then user.save, double-counting each signup attempt.
app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — match_count increment is a non-atomic read-modify-write, so concurrent signups lose updates; use update_counters/increment_counter.

adjudication.rationale: In app/models/blocked_email.rb `should_block?` does `record = BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` then `record.match_count += 1` and `record.save`. This is a classic non-atomic read-modify-write; concurrent signups hitting the same blocked email can overwrite each other’s increments and lose updates to `match_count` (and potentially `last_match_at`). Using `update_counters`/`increment_counter` (or a single SQL UPDATE) would avoid the race. This behavior is directly present in the added model code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:16 — Return value of record.save is ignored and runs inside the caller's transaction, so counter updates silently fail or roll back with the failed user save.

adjudication.rationale: In BlockedEmail.should_block? the code mutates match_count/last_match_at and calls record.save, but ignores the return value and doesn’t handle/save! on failure (app/models/blocked_email.rb:13-18). This means the “statistics” update can silently not persist (e.g., validation/db failure), and since it’s invoked from EmailValidator during user validation, it may also be subject to whatever transactional context the caller uses, potentially losing the counter update. The diff clearly shows ignored save/error handling; the exact transaction/rollback behavior is not fully verifiable from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:5 — BlockedEmail uniqueness validation and unique index are case-sensitive, allowing duplicate entries differing only by case with inconsistent action_type.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `BlockedEmail` with `validates :email, uniqueness: true` (default case-sensitive) and a DB unique index on `:email` with no case-insensitive handling (`add_index :blocked_emails, :email, unique: true`). `BlockedEmail.should_block?` also does an exact-match lookup (`where(email: email).first`). With no normalization (e.g., downcasing) shown, entries like `Spam@Example.com` and `spam@example.com` can coexist (or fail to match depending on input casing), leading to inconsistent action_type/statistics and allowing blocked emails to bypass blocking by changing case.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:275 — Any email error (e.g. already taken or transient) permanently adds the email to rejectedEmails client-side, showing a generic "invalid" reason and blocking resubmission until reload.

adjudication.rationale: In create_account_controller.js, on any failed signup response that includes `result.errors.email`, the code unconditionally `pushObject(result.values.email)` into `rejectedEmails` (new state on the controller). The email validation then short-circuits: if `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` it returns a failed validation with reason `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, regardless of the actual server-side error (e.g. uniqueness, domain restriction, blocked). Because `rejectedEmails` persists for the controller lifetime, the same email will remain blocked client-side until the controller is reloaded/reset, preventing resubmission for that email even if the server-side condition was transient or changed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:198 — New `errors`/`values` keys in users#create failure JSON have no controller spec, so the contract the client now depends on (errors.email + values.email) is unverified and can drift silently.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes `users#create` failure JSON to include `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice(...)`, and the client (`create_account_controller.js`) now explicitly depends on `result.errors.email` and `result.values.email` to populate `rejectedEmails`. The diff does not add any request/controller spec asserting this response shape, so this new client-visible contract isn’t directly verified in tests here and could change without detection.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:274 — Client treats any `errors.email` entry (taken, format, whitelist, blocked) as a permanent per-session rejection because the response gives no error code to distinguish blocked emails from other failures.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, after a failed create, any response containing `result.errors.email` causes `result.values.email` to be pushed into `rejectedEmails` (lines ~271-274). Later, `emailValidation` hard-fails if `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` and returns the generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` reason, without inspecting which email error occurred. The server response added in `users_controller.rb` only includes `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: ...slice(...)`—no error codes—so the client cannot distinguish `blocked` vs `not_allowed` vs `taken`, etc. This is a real, diff-grounded UX/behavior concern (over-broad per-session caching and generic messaging), but it doesn’t clearly break correctness since those emails are still invalid for account creation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:206 — Other users#create failure branches (StatementInvalid, NicknameUnavailable) return a different response shape without `errors`/`values`, so the failure contract is inconsistent across paths.

adjudication.rationale: In users_controller#create, the main validation-failure JSON render was changed to include `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice(...)`, but the method still has other failure exits (e.g., the `rescue ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid` shown in the diff, and likely other exception branches) that are not updated here. That makes the failure response shape inconsistent across paths, which matters because the new client logic in `create_account_controller.js` conditionally relies on `result.errors`/`result.values` to cache rejected emails.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — should_block? mutates match_count/last_match_at as a side effect of validation, so every valid? call (e.g. valid? then save) double-counts matches, even when the validation outcome is discarded

adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both point to the same core problem: the predicate/check method (`should_block?` / `should_block_email?`) performs side effects by mutating tracking fields (e.g., `match_count`, `last_match_at`) during what should be a read-only decision. The candidate additionally notes a concrete consequence (double-counting when `valid?` is called multiple times), which is consistent with the golden concern about unintended side effects and concurrency risks.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — match_count is incremented via read-modify-write (record.match_count += 1; save) instead of an atomic update, losing counts under concurrent signups

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (new file `app/models/blocked_email.rb`), when a record exists it does `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save`. This is a classic read-modify-write sequence that is not atomic; concurrent signups hitting the same blocked email can overwrite each other’s increments, causing lost updates in `match_count`/`last_match_at` statistics. The diff clearly shows this non-atomic update pattern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:17 — rejectedEmails: Em.A([]) is defined on the prototype so the array is shared across all controller instances and never reset between modal openings

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is created once at class definition time inside `Discourse.Controller.extend(...)`, so it becomes a shared mutable default (array) on the prototype. The diff then mutates it via `get('rejectedEmails').pushObject(...)` on failed signup, and uses it in validation (`contains(email)`), meaning rejected emails can leak across controller instances / lifetimes instead of being fresh per modal/use. The diff shows no reset/initialization per instance/open, so the finding is grounded and can cause persistent/incorrect client-side invalidation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:10 — Unique index and BlockedEmail lookup on email are case-sensitive and emails are never normalized, so "Foo@x.com" bypasses a block on "foo@x.com" and case-variant duplicates can be stored.

adjudication.rationale: The new BlockedEmail feature matches and enforces uniqueness using exact string equality: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and a DB unique index on `:email` in the migration. The diff shows no normalization (e.g., downcasing) of the email before storing or querying, and Rails `validates ... uniqueness: true` is case-sensitive by default. Therefore `Foo@x.com` would not match a blocked `foo@x.com`, and case-variant duplicates can be inserted despite the uniqueness constraint.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — match_count is incremented via read-modify-write and save rather than an atomic update, so concurrent matches lose counts.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, when a record exists it does `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save` (read-modify-write). Under concurrent calls for the same email, two processes can read the same `match_count`, both increment, and the later save overwrites the earlier, losing increments. This non-atomic update is visible in the added `app/models/blocked_email.rb` logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — should_block? does exact case-sensitive match on unnormalized email (User.new_from_params does not downcase/strip), so "Bad@x.com" or " bad@x.com" bypasses the block

adjudication.rationale: BlockedEmail.should_block?(email) queries with `where(email: email)` (app/models/blocked_email.rb:12) and EmailValidator passes the raw `value` without any normalization/strip/downcase (lib/validators/email_validator.rb). The diff shows no normalization step for `User.email` before validation, so blocked-email enforcement is exact-string and can be bypassed by case/whitespace variants if those reach validation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:20 — Domain regex only escapes "." and is unanchored at the end, so whitelist "example.com" accepts attacker@example.com.evil.org and other regex metachars in settings are injected verbatim

adjudication.rationale: In lib/validators/email_validator.rb, email_in_restriction_setting? builds `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` after only escaping dots via `setting.gsub('.', '\.')`. This regex is not end-anchored, so a whitelist entry like `example.com` will match `attacker@example.com.evil.org` (it contains `@example.com` as a substring). Also, because only `.` is escaped, other regex metacharacters present in the setting (e.g. `+`, `*`, `|`, `(`, `)`, `[`) will be interpreted by the Regexp engine rather than treated as literals, enabling unintended matches/bypasses. The diff adds this validator logic as new code, so the issue is verifiable from the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:198 — Distinct "blocked" error now returned in errors hash lets unauthenticated callers probe which emails are on the admin blocklist

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new blocked-email check (`EmailValidator` adds `I18n.t(:'user.email.blocked')` when `BlockedEmail.should_block?` matches) and changes `UsersController#create` to return `errors: user.errors.to_hash` to the client on failed signup. That makes the specific email error message (e.g., the new `user.email.blocked` vs other email failures like `user.email.not_allowed`) directly observable by unauthenticated callers, enabling programmatic probing of which emails are present in the admin-managed `blocked_emails` table.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:4 — Whitelist/blacklist domain logic moved from User into EmailValidator but the validator spec has no whitelist/blacklist cases, so the relocated behavior is untested here.

adjudication.rationale: The diff removes the domain whitelist/blacklist checks from `User#email_validator` and reimplements them in `lib/validators/email_validator.rb` (`SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist` / `email_domains_blacklist`). However, `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb` only covers the new `BlockedEmail.should_block?` branch and has no examples exercising the whitelist/blacklist setting behavior, leaving the relocated logic untested in this spec.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — No test covers the guard that skips the BlockedEmail check (and its match_count side effect) when a whitelist/blacklist error already exists.

adjudication.rationale: EmailValidator#validate_each only calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value) when `record.errors[attribute].blank?` (line with `and BlockedEmail.should_block?`), meaning whitelist/blacklist failures should skip the blocked-email check and its match_count/last_match_at side effects. The added spec `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb` only stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? for the “blocked email” contexts and does not cover a whitelist/blacklist error case to assert BlockedEmail.should_block? is not invoked when an earlier restriction error is present.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb:11 — Both blocked-email tests stub BlockedEmail.should_block?, so nothing checks the validator against a real BlockedEmail record or the actual error message.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb` stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?` in both examples (`returns(false)` and `returns(true)`), so the validator spec doesn’t exercise interaction with an actual `BlockedEmail` DB record or verify the specific translated error (`user.email.blocked`); it only checks `record.errors[:email]` presence/absence. While `spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb` covers `should_block?`, the validator’s end-to-end behavior with real records/message isn’t covered here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:198 — The create failure response gained new errors/values keys (which expose user attributes) with no controller spec asserting their shape or contents.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show the create failure JSON gaining `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` in `app/controllers/users_controller.rb`, but it does not show whether controller/request specs exist elsewhere asserting this response shape. Absence of tests cannot be verified from the provided diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:274 — The new rejectedEmails client logic (push on server email error, then fail emailValidation) has no JS test.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new client-side behavior in `create_account_controller.js`: a `rejectedEmails` array, emailValidation short-circuiting when `rejectedEmails.contains(email)`, dependency on `rejectedEmails.@each`, and pushing `result.values.email` on server-side email errors (around the referenced line). In the diff, only Ruby/model/validator specs are added; there are no new JS/QUnit/Ember tests covering this new rejected-emails flow, so the finding is specific and diff-grounded (missing test for newly added nontrivial client logic), but not itself a runtime defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/user.rb:47 — Switching to `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` has no User-level spec confirming blocked emails are rejected on create and skipped when the email is unchanged.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes User email validation from a custom `email_validator` to `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` (app/models/user.rb). The new `EmailValidator` adds blocked-email behavior via `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, but the added specs only cover `EmailValidator` in isolation (spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb) and `BlockedEmail` (spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb). There is no User-level spec exercising user creation/update to confirm (a) blocked emails are rejected during `User` validation on create and (b) the validator is skipped when the email is unchanged, which is a meaningful behavioral contract introduced by the `if: :email_changed?` condition.
